title: Command safety and help

sources.locator: NIST Secure Software Development Framework; SP 800-218 v1.1; section applicable to Command safety and help
sources.claim: Safe shell work scopes destructive commands to verified literal paths, previews targets, preserves recoverable copies, and avoids constructing commands from untrusted text.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Some commands can't be undone: `rm -rf` deletes without a recycle bin, `>` overwrites a file, and a wrong path in either can wipe real work. Safe habits: **preview** the targets first (`ls` the exact path, or `rm -ri` to confirm each), use **literal, quoted paths** you've checked with `pwd`, **never** build destructive commands from text you didn't write (a filename, a web page, an AI answer) without reading it, and keep a **recoverable copy** (commit or stash in Git, or copy to a backup) before bulk changes. When unsure what a command does, read its **help** (`man rm`, `rm --help`, `Get-Help Remove-Item`) before running it.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner wants to delete the project's build output. They type `rm -rf $BUILD_DIR/*`, but BUILD_DIR isn't set in this terminal, so the command becomes `rm -rf /*`. They notice just before pressing Enter; run as written, it would try to delete everything their account can reach.Before a recursive cleanup, the learner resolves and prints the intended build directory and removes only that verified path inside the repository. In this lesson you'll review a risky command sequence and propose a verifiable safer workflow.

```predict
{"question": "The path in a delete command \"looks about right\". Is that enough to run it?", "options": ["Yes, if you've used the command before", "No: print and check the exact resolved path first"], "answer": 1, "why": "Deletion is immediate and permanent in the shell. Verify, then act."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Files, folders and paths** and **Create, copy, move and rename** (exact sources, destinations and verification).

sections.heading: The rule: resolve, preview, then act on the verified path
sections.body:
```bash
# Risky: variable may be empty; glob may match more than intended.
# rm -rf $BUILD_DIR/*

# Safer.
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"   # start at the repo root.
target="./dist"                           # a literal path inside the repo.
[ -d "$target" ] || { echo "no $target"; exit 1; }   # stop if it isn't there.
ls -la "$target"                          # preview what will go.
rm -r -- "$target"                        # remove only that folder; -- ends options.

git clean -n                              # preview untracked files Git would delete.
git clean -f                              # only after reading the preview.
```

| Risk | Safer habit |
|---|---|
| empty or wrong variable. | print it; use `${VAR:?}` to stop if empty. |
| broad globs like `*`. | `ls` the glob first to see the matches. |
| overwriting with `>`. | check the filename; use `>>` to append. |
| pasted commands. | read every part; never pipe unknown scripts to a shell. |
| no way back. | commit or stash first; keep a copy. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "What does `${BUILD_DIR:?}` do?", "answer": "It stops the command with an error if BUILD_DIR is empty or unset, so rm never runs on the wrong path."}
```

sections.heading: Help before harm

includes: Preview and verify targets before destructive commands, using literal quoted paths.
Use dry runs, help pages and recoverable copies; avoid building commands from untrusted text.
excludes: Shell scripting best practices in depth.

outcomes: Review a risky command sequence and propose a verifiable safer workflow.

examples.title: Cleaning the build folder, and only the build folder
examples.situation: Before a recursive cleanup, the learner resolves and prints the intended build directory and removes only that verified path inside the repository.
walkthrough: **Resolve and print the build directory:** from the repo root, target="./dist" and `ls -la ./dist` shows only generated files.
**Remove only that verified path:** `rm -r -- ./dist` deletes that folder and nothing else in the repository.
**Check:** git status will show no tracked files lost, and the next build recreates dist/.
examples.result: Build output is cleaned reliably, with no chance of deleting source code or anything outside the repo.

examples.title: The helpful one-liner from a forum
examples.situation: A forum post suggests `curl http://example.com/fix.sh | sudo bash` to fix a build error.
walkthrough: That runs unknown code with full admin rights before anyone reads it.
Download the script to a file, read it, and understand each command.
Prefer the project's documented fix, or run the needed steps yourself in a disposable environment.
examples.result: The build is fixed without running unreviewed code as administrator.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A familiar delete command is safe to run immediately if the typed path looks approximately correct.
misconceptions.correction: Shell deletion has no undo, and small differences (an empty variable, a stray space, the wrong folder) change what gets deleted. Resolve and preview the exact path, then act only on that.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Cleaning the build folder, and only the build folder", what did the empty variable turn the command into?

analogy.example: Running a destructive command is like **using a paper shredder**: before feeding it, you look at exactly which pages are in your hand. A dry run is **reading the list of pages first**; a commit or backup is **keeping a photocopy** in case you shred the wrong one.
usefulFor: dry run = read the list first
limitations: Shredders are slow enough to stop; rm -rf isn't.
A pasted command is someone else's stack of pages; read them first.

remediation.explanation: Before any destructive command, run the three checks: **print the resolved path, preview the matches, and make sure there's a way back.** If a command came from someone else, read every part first.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The helpful one-liner from a forum".

recap.summary: To review a risky command sequence and propose a safer workflow, resolve and print exact paths, preview matches with ls or dry-run flags, use quoted literal paths and guards for empty variables, keep a recoverable copy, read help pages when unsure, and never run commands built from untrusted text without reading them.
